Ozun and Ogún are jointly received in the Cuban Warrior complex.
Ellis lists Ọ̀ṣun among Ogun's siblings born from Yemọja.

Ellis lists Ọya among Ogun's siblings born from Yemọja.

Ellis lists Ṣàngó among Ogun's siblings born from Yemọja.

Ògún emerges from Yemoja in Ellis’s birth list.
An Oyo-related tradition says Ogun could not sustain his marriage with Yemọja.
Cuban traditions make Ogun husband or companion of Yemayá Okuté.

relations.myth: Oraniyan raises Oke from the primordial sea
relations.note: Ọlọ́fin empowers Oraniyan to bring Oke, the first mountain, above the waters.

relations.note: Oke rises from waters belonging to Olokun, spatially displacing the primordial sea.

Some Brazilian Efọn traditions describe Olooke as Oxum's father and fellow patron.

relations.note: The mountain deity Òkè emerges from Yemoja.
Olodumare assigns Olókun the sea or recognizes Olókun's governance of it.
Olódùmarè bestows, approves, seals, or witnesses the destiny borne by Orí.
Orí may approach Olódùmarè as an advocate for its human owner.
Olódùmarè sends Ọ̀rúnmìlà among the heavenly beings commissioned to descend.
Olodumare gives Ifá to Orunmila so divine wisdom can reach humanity.
Olódùmarè grants or recognizes his access to prenatal destinies.
Olodumare summons Orunmila, who explains that destiny prevented the desired outcome.
Olodumare sends Orunmila to earth to teach wisdom and reveal sacrifices.
Olodumare orders Ọ̀rúnmìlà and three other divinities to extend humanity.
Olodumare summons Orunmila to solve divine problems with specialist wisdom.
Some matricide variants place Oshosi’s promise concerning stolen game before Olódùmarè.
Some one-arrow variants make the supreme deity reward Oshosi’s successful shot.

relations.myth: The excluded woman and failed creation
relations.note: Olódùmarè orders the male powers to recognize and include Ọ̀ṣun.
relations.source: Abimbola and Abiodun, Ọ̀ṣun across the Waters

relations.note: Ọ̀ṣun reaches Olódùmarè as a vulture, enabling rain and restoration.

Priestly exegesis links the rainbow to Olodumare's luminous pot and created world.

Olódùmarè grants or ratifies Ṣàngó’s thunder power or divine status.
Iemanjá helps Olodumare create the world in Brazilian narratives.
Modern diaspora narratives describe Oko as married to Olokun.
Oko reveals Olokun's sex or hermaphroditism in modern diaspora narratives.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà consults or aids Olókun in narratives of wealth and aquatic danger.

Cuban Ifá establishes communication with Olokun through Orula's consecrated instruments.

relations.source: Recorded Ifá and Cuban ritual discourse

Olókun emerges from Yemoja’s ruptured body.

Some Cuban and transnational traditions make Olokun an older road or manifestation of Yemayá.
Atlantic systems may make Olókun her abyssal counterpart or complement.
Some Cuban houses describe Olokun as Yemayá's parent.
Yemayá governs visible coastal waters while Olokun governs the deep ocean.

relations.myth: Olókun gives masks to Yewá and Oyá
relations.note: Olókun gives Yewá a ritual mask.
Regional narratives place Yewá with Olókun in or beside the sea.
One Cuban family genealogy makes Olókun Yewá's sibling.
An Ifá-associated verse says Ori established or created Oko at Agba Irawo.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà witnesses destiny and interprets the prenatal course embodied by Orí.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà interprets the destiny borne by Orí and urges clients to honor it.

Later pantheon lists call Oko a husband or former husband of Ọya.

Ellis reports that Oko sprang from Yemoja's body.
Òrìṣà Oko emerges from Yemoja in Ellis’s birth list.
Later Yoruba and diasporic lists describe Yemoja as Oko's wife.
Yemayá seduces the chaste farmer Oko to obtain his cultivation secret.
Yemayá takes Oko's secret knowledge of yam cultivation.

relations.myth: Return of the corpse to earth
relations.note: Yewá's reduction of the corpse prepares its incorporation into Orisha Oko.

relations.myth: Return of the corpse to earth
relations.note: Bolívar instead assigns corpse consumption to Orisha Oko after transfer through Oyá.

Ọ̀rúnmìlà rejects offerings presented by Ossaim.

Ọ̀rúnmìlà purchases or owns Ossaim as a slave in Brazilian narratives.

Ọ̀rúnmìlà grants or controls Ossaim's access to leaf power.

relations.myth: The bag of wisdom and divination
relations.note: They collaborate in divination, and he acknowledges or authorizes her related system.
Several traditions describe Ọ̀ṣun as Ọ̀rúnmìlà's wife.

relations.myth: The bag of wisdom and divination

relations.note: Some variants say Ọ̀ṣun secretly learns or acquires his divinatory wisdom.
After Ọ̀rúnmìlà sacrifices to avoid removal to heaven, the messenger becomes his helper or staff.
A widespread account presents Ọ̀ṣun as Ọ̀rúnmìlà’s wife.
Regional narratives place Ọ̀rúnmìlà and Ṣàngó as rival husbands involving Ọ̀ṣun.
Osun serves as Ọ̀rúnmìlà’s staff, altar, insignia, messenger, and executor of Ifá’s prescriptions.

relations.note: Ọ̀rúnmìlà teaches Ọ̀ṣun, whose practice becomes the sixteen-cowrie oracle.
Counter-traditions make Ọ̀ṣun the source from whom Ọ̀rúnmìlà learns divinatory power.
Some traditions add Ọ̀rúnmìlà among Ọya's husbands or lovers.
Ifá prescribes the sacrifice or treatment enabling Ọya to bear nine children.
Regional Ọ̀ṣun traditions portray Ọ̀rúnmìlà and Ṣàngó as rival husbands.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà prescribes sacrifice; Ṣàngó prospers through obedience or falls through refusal.
Ifá warns Ṣàngó and prescribes sacrifices before political and magical disasters.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà divines for Ṣàngó in royal and conflict narratives.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà initiates Ṣàngó into Ifá and teaches the controlled use of power.
Some Cuban narratives make Yemayá his wife and connect her with restricted divination.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà’s divination links worshippers to offerings involving Yemoja.
After rescuing Ọ̀rúnmìlà, Yewa marries him and bears a son.

Ọ̀rúnmìlà arrives with Yemayá and witnesses Yewá's skeletal secret.

relations.myth: Yewa vanishes in the raffia forest
relations.note: Ifá warns Yewa to sacrifice before traveling, but she refuses.

relations.myth: The chaste daughters of Yewá and Olósa
relations.note: Ọ̀rúnmìlà advises Yewá and Olósa concerning Lashure's disruption.
Other Cuban accounts describe Ochosi and Osain working closely together.
Ossaim lures, enchants, drugs, or captures Oxóssi, who remains in his forest.

Some tellings say Ossaim teaches the captured or enchanted Oxóssi.
Cuban accounts say Ochosi receives knowledge of forest plants from Osain.
Ọ̀ṣun takes medicinal leaves from Ọ̀sányìn's grinding stone, asserting medical knowledge.
Brazilian mythographic genealogy groups Ossaim and Oxumarê as siblings.
Ọya's gale opens Ossaim's container and scatters his stored leaves.
Osain provides Changó with a magical medicine, gourd, or secret.
Ṣàngó demands that Ossaim's monopolized leaf knowledge be shared among the orishas.
Osanyin prepares the herbal potion that ends Yewá's pregnancy.
Brazilian genealogy makes Ossaim a sibling of Euá.
Brazilian Ketu narratives make Oxum Oshosi’s lover or consort.
Some Cuban and Brazilian houses describe Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì as her husband or companion.
Oxum attracts the elusive hunter using honey, beauty, or forest leaves.
Osun and Ochosi belong to the fourfold Cuban warrior initiation package.
Ozun and Ochosi are jointly received in the Cuban Warrior complex.

Oshosi emerges from Yemaja’s ruptured body as one of her offspring.
Some traditions portray them as allied powerful female water and wind beings.
Ọ̀ṣun and Ọya appear as rival co-wives or companions of Ṣàngó.

Her freshwater, diplomacy, beauty, and wealth sometimes contest his heat and virility.
Some genealogies name Yemọja as Ọ̀ṣun's mother.

Òṣùmàrè serves Ṣàngó by returning fallen rainwater to the clouds.
In Cuba, Ochumare survives as Yemayá’s crown, linked to the sea-born rainbow.

Modern systematization calls Euá female Oxumarê or his serpent counterpart.
Oxumarê hides or shelters Euá.
Brazilian traditions commonly call Oxumarê Euá's brother.
Ọ̀ṣun Apará envies Ọya in a diasporic narrative.
Ọya entrusts her Ìbejì children to Ọ̀ṣun, who raises them.
A regional genealogy says Ọya was born or raised in Ọ̀ṣun's house.
A regional diasporic version has Ọ̀ṣun seduce Ọya.
Ọya and Ọ̀ṣun are co-wives of Ṣàngó alongside Obà.
Ọ̀ṣun is Ṣàngó’s attractive, diplomatic, or favored wife in numerous traditions.

She fights beside him and is indispensable to his victory.
Ọya fights beside Ṣàngó and commands winds and storms preceding his thunder.
Ọya is his faithful wife and storm-weather counterpart.

She steals or tastes his fire medicine and gains fire-spitting power.
Some Atlantic genealogical charts name Yemọja as Ọya's mother.
Ọya emerges from Yemoja in Ellis’s birth list.
In another system Oyá receives the dead before Yewá acts deeper inside.
In one system Yewá brings or passes the dead to Oyá.
Ọya and Ewá belong to the cemetery-associated trio of female orishas.

Ellis’s cosmic genealogy and many Cuban houses make Yemọja Ṣàngó’s mother.

Yewá grants Yemayá and her children privileged access to her secret.
Yemayá feeds Yewá's sons and later discovers Yewá among bones.

Abatá.note: Some Cuban lineages identify Abatá as Inle's wife.
Cuban lineages variously call Abatá Inle's sister, older sister, or younger counterpart.
Some houses describe Abatá and Inle as twins.
Abatá is Inle's assistant, aquatic counterpart, and inseparable ritual companion in some lineages.

Abatá.myth: Healing fish for Abatá's blind father
Abatá.note: Inle calms the sea and supplies the healing fish sought by Abatá.

Adamó.note: The great blue serpent Adamó guards Inle, Abatá, and their family.

Agayú.note: A devotional website calls Agayú Oke's brother and volcanic counterpart without older corroboration.

Agboni.note: Yewá bears Agboni by Bromú; Oddudúa recovers and raises him.

Agemo.note: Soyinka joins Ogun's road-and-metal complex with the Ijebu transitional masquerade Agemo.

Aggayú.note: A bullock was sacrificed for Aggayú beneath the Socorro ceiba also called Iroko.

Agé.note: Regional forest-healing spirit compared or historically fused with Ọ̀sányìn.

Ajagun.note: Ogbomoso tradition calls Oba Ajagun’s partner; Ajagun is associated with Ṣàngó.

Ajalayé.note: As Ajalọ́run, Olodumare contests senior female Earth, who prevails through seniority.

Ajalọ́run.note: A regional cosmology identifies Olodumare with the male sky principle Ajalọ́run.

Aje.note: A female butcher consulted Aje through Ogun and her iron tools.

Ajé.myth: Ajé consults Ifá for enduring prosperity
Ajé.note: The Odù direct wealth through sacrifices and good character necessary to retain prosperity.
Ajé is brought from or personified within Olokun's wealthy aquatic domain.
Ajé.source: Yoruba praise and modern ritual literature

Ajé.note: Some modern devotees identify the personified wealth-power as Ajé Olókun, though the equation is not universal.

Ajé Ṣaluga.note: The wealth deity Ajé Ṣaluga emerges from Yemoja.

Akaró.note: Akaró accompanies Olokun, represents death, and is commonly paired with Somú Gagá.

Akódá.myth: Ifá descends and gains early transmitters
Akódá.note: Akódá becomes an early disciple and authoritative transmitter of the Odù corpus.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà teaches Akódá as an early or first pupil and assistant.
Akódá serves Ọ̀rúnmìlà as an early assistant in widely circulated accounts.

Alajeru.note: Scattered modern parentage accounts name Alajeru as a parent of Ọ̀rúnmìlà.

Allah.note: Muslim Yoruba use Ọlọ́run for Allah as a lived theological translation.

Angorô.note: Brazilian Angola-nation traditions place this Bantu rainbow-serpent power in correspondence with Oxumaré.

Anyiewo.note: Ellis compares Òṣùmàrè with the neighboring Ewe rainbow-serpent Anyiewo.

Archangel Michael.note: Some Pernambuco and other Brazilian settings correspond Oxóssi with Archangel Michael.

Arámfè.note: Odúwa participates in the divine descent directed by Arámfè.

Asesú.myth: Yewá and Asesú live at sea
Asesú.note: Yewá and Asesú live together in a boat at sea.

Aṣedá.myth: Ifá descends and gains early transmitters
Aṣedá.note: Aṣedá becomes an early disciple and authoritative transmitter of the Odù corpus.

Aṣẹ̀dá.note: Ọ̀rúnmìlà teaches Aṣẹ̀dá as an early or first pupil and assistant.
Aṣẹ̀dá serves Ọ̀rúnmìlà as an early assistant in widely circulated accounts.

Baphomet.note: Modern occult systems sometimes identify Èṣù with Baphomet without historical basis.

Bessém.note: Jeje-Brazilian liturgy places Bessém in correspondence with Oxumaré.

Boromú.note: Afro-Cuban Ifá houses place Boromú beside Oddúa as an ancient funerary power.

Bromú.note: Bromú becomes Yewá's secret lover and impregnates her.
Bromú initially serves as one of imprisoned Yewá's guardians.
Some Cuban versions make Bromú Yewá's son after Ṣàngó violates her.

Brosiá.note: Afro-Cuban Ifá houses place Brosiá with Oddúa among primordial funerary powers.
Brosiá guards imprisoned Yewá, then betrays her secret to Oddudúa.
Some Cuban versions make Brosiá Yewá's child after Ṣàngó violates her.

Caboclos.note: In many Umbanda houses, Caboclo spirits work under Oxóssi’s line or vibration.

Cosmas and Damian.note: Afro-Catholic traditions identify or ritually associate the twins with these physician-martyr saints.

Crianças.note: Umbanda associates Ibeji with child-spirit lines or phalanxes manifesting through mediums.

Deus.note: Some Umbanda traditions use Olorum alongside or as the Christian Deus.

Elédàá.note: Cuban Lucumí discourse sometimes equates Eledá with Orí, though other houses distinguish them.

Ere.myth: The subterranean serpent drinks from heaven
Ere.note: The sacred python Ere serves as Òṣùmàrè’s messenger.

Erês.note: Brazilian traditions overlap Ibeji with childlike ritual entities, though they remain theologically distinct.

Euá.note: Brazilian mythographic genealogy groups Ossaim and Euá as siblings.

Ewá.note: Regional Brazilian classifications name Ewá among Nanã's children.
Some Brazilian genealogies describe Ewá as Òṣùmàrè’s sister or twin.
In one collected Brazilian narrative, Oxumaré hides Ewá.

Hohovi.note: Fon and Ewe divine twins compared with Ibeji and proposed as historically influential.

Hêviosso.note: A minority of Beninese respondents identified an iroko tree with Hêviosso.

Ibúalámo.note: Some houses treat Ibúalámo as a fused form or quality of Oshosi.

Iku.note: Contemporary theology associates him with Iku because he may deliver sufferers to death or withhold them.

Ikú.note: Ikú, Death, precedes or commands the other Ajogun as their foremost and gravest member.
They alternate music secretly, appearing inexhaustible until Death concedes or flees.
Contemporary retellings say Nanã conceals, restrains, or houses Death.

Ikú.myth: Death is negotiated through an Odù
Ikú.note: Odù prescriptions negotiate, delay, or accept death, with outcomes differing among narratives.

Some Cuban stories make personified Death seek or marry Ọya.
Ikú threatens or negotiates with Ọya over cemetery custody and its threshold.
Yewa thwarts Ikú's pursuit of Ọ̀rúnmìlà.

Imadese.note: A modern-recorded Edo narrative says Olókun meets or marries Imadese Mammy Wata.

Iwà.note: Personified Iwà is Ọ̀rúnmìlà’s wife in an ethical divinatory narrative.
After mistreatment, Iwà leaves Ọ̀rúnmìlà and his well-being disappears with her.

Iyamase.note: Gantois-linked mythology names Iyamase as mother of Dadá and Xangô.

Iyámi Oxorongá.note: Recent accounts say Iyámi Oxorongá gives Logun Edé a bow and magical formulas.

Jakuta.note: Scattered modern parentage accounts name Jakuta as a parent of Ọ̀rúnmìlà.
Sources equate Ṣàngó with Jakuta, possibly fusing a royal ancestor with an older thunder deity.

Jesus Christ.note: Bahian and Umbanda traditions publicly correlate Oxalá with Christ, especially Senhor do Bonfim.

Joan of Arc.note: Modern Brazilian Umbanda equates Oba with Joan as an embattled woman.

Katendê.note: Mixed-nation Candomblé and Umbanda sometimes equate this Angola-Congo leaf deity with Ossaim.

Kohosu.note: An Abomey genealogy names Nàná Bùkùú as Kohosu's mother.

La Caridad del Cobre.note: Cuban practice pairs Ochún with the Marian image as analogous, co-present, or identical.

Lagelu.myth: Lagelu and his people take refuge on Oke-Ibadan
Lagelu.note: Oke-Ibadan shelters Lagelu's refugees and covenants to protect and nourish their community.
Lagelu.source: Ibadan oral history and festival ethnography

Langa.note: The Adele migration legend names Langa as Brukung's servant during the cult's withdrawal and migration.

Legba.note: Èṣù and Fon-Ewe Legba belong to related traditions shaped by regional contact and ritual exchange.

Lisa.note: Some Fon and Jeje theological systems describe Loko as Lisa’s firstborn.
Nana Buluku brings forth male Lisa before the ordered cosmos.

Mami Wata.note: Contemporary Nigerian practice sometimes overlaps or equates them, though other practitioners distinguish them.
Some practitioners associate the aquatic powers, though their histories remain distinct.

Mawu.note: Some Fon and Jeje theological systems describe Loko as Mawu’s firstborn.
Nana Buluku brings forth female Mawu before the ordered cosmos.
Nana Buluku assigns Mawu dominion over night and the moon.

Nossa Senhora da Conceição.note: Some Brazilian traditions correspond Iemanjá with Nossa Senhora da Conceição.

Nossa Senhora dos Navegantes.note: Some Brazilian regions correspond Iemanjá with this Marian maritime figure.

Nuestra Señora de Monserrate.note: Some Cuban houses identify Yewá with this Marian figure.

Nuestra Señora de los Desamparados.note: Some Cuban houses identify Yewá with this Marian figure.

Nuestra Señora del Rosario.note: Some Cuban lineages identify Dadá-Bañani with Nuestra Señora del Rosario.

Nyohwe Ananu.note: An Abomey genealogy makes Nàná mother of Nyohwe Ananu.

Obalufon.note: Modern-recorded Ife dynastic traditions attach Ogun to conflicts involving Obalufon.

Obba.note: Cuban genealogies make Obba and Yewá daughters of Oddudúa.
Obba guards the grave while Yewá acts within corpse or sepulcher.

Odé.note: Odé may designate Oshosi, another hunter divinity, a title, or hunters collectively.

Odù.note: Some priests identify Odù, womb and source of existence, with the essence of àjẹ́.

Odù.myth: Female Odù bears the principal signs
Odù.note: Female Odù bears or encompasses the principal Odù and governs their mystery.
Odù marries Ọ̀rúnmìlà and joins him as a powerful ritual partner.
In variants, Odù brings or teaches secret divinatory knowledge to Ọ̀rúnmìlà.
Their ritual alliance depends on his promise to conceal Odù’s presence or vessel.

Odù.myth: The excluded woman and failed creation
Odù.note: Ọ̀ṣun is interpreted as the hidden female Odù enabling the sixteenfold system.

Odúa-dúa.note: Agayú carries the supernatural child Odúa-dúa across a flooded river.

Oggué.note: Oke joins Oggué and Orisha Oko in a functional triad of earth-related powers.
Modern Cuban manuals group Oko, Oke, and Oggué over agriculture, terrain, and livestock.

Ogodo.note: Ogodo’s weaker thunder contrasts with Aganju’s sharp, whip-like cracks.

Ogué.note: Ogué is ritually present in lineage-specific initiation sequences for Agayú initiates.

Ojúmu.note: At Odúwa’s command, Ojúmu distributes sand and releases the five-clawed bird.

Okere.note: Okere is Yemoja’s husband in the Ìsẹ́yìn water narrative.
Okere breaks her taboo or insults her, causing her departure and flood.

Olofi.note: Olofi creates Ozun as an ever-wakeful sentinel charged to observe danger.
Cuban theology describes Ozun as Olofi’s messenger or sentinel.

Olofin.note: Some variants make Olofin the divine king who rewards Oshosi.
Òṣùmàrè works as Olofin’s diviner every four days for meager pay.
Olofin later compensates Òṣùmàrè generously and gives him red clothing.

Olofin.myth: The chaste daughters of Yewá and Olósa
Olofin.note: Olofin authoritatively decrees rules concerning men approaching their daughters.

Olókun Seniade.note: Òṣùmàrè divines for Olókun Seniade, prescribing a successful sacrifice.

Olósa.note: The lagoon deity Olósa emerges from Yemoja.

Olósa.myth: The chaste daughters of Yewá and Olósa
Olósa.note: They share a lagoon, receive offerings, and respond jointly to Lashure.

Olúfọ̀n.note: Brazilian theology incorporates the Ifọ̀n deity as the elderly form of Oxalá.

Olúwéré.note: Regional accounts name Olúwéré as the iroko spirit receiving Olúrónbí’s vow.

Omi Logun.note: Omi Logun is one of Yewá's two named sons.

Omitogun.note: Omitogun is one of Yewá's two named sons.

Onílẹ̀.note: Olodumare grants the initially overlooked or concealed Onílẹ̀ the earth itself.

Opará.note: Some Brazilian accounts call Opará the daughter of Oba and Xangô.

Oraniyan.myth: Oraniyan raises Oke from the primordial sea
Oraniyan.note: Oraniyan raises Oke from beneath the sea, producing the first dry land.

Orishala.note: Oshosi supplies animals killed for Orishala’s use.
Orishala rewards Oshosi with a magnificent beaded gown and, in variants, cap and trousers.
Some variants make Oshosi Orishala’s spokesman or intermediary.

Oroíña.note: Some Cuban traditions make Agayú the son of earth’s fiery interior, Oroíña.
Other Cuban traditions pair Agayú with Oroíña as connected elemental powers.

Orungan.note: Orungan is the son of Aganju and Yemoja.
Orungan’s pursuit of Yemaja precipitates the rupture from which Oshosi emerges.
Orungan assaults or attempts to rape Yemoja, then pursues her.

Orò.note: Egúngún and Orò are paired but distinct; Egúngún appears publicly while Orò is nocturnal and restrictive.
Some communities and practitioners describe Orò as a complementary male counterforce to the Mothers.

Osanobua.note: Edo tradition commonly describes Olókun as the creator's child or subordinate.
Osanobua.source: Edo oral accounts collected by Izevbigie

Osanobua.note: The creator assigns Olókun dominion over the sea and sometimes grants status, wealth, or a spouse.
Osanobua.source: Edo oral accounts collected by Izevbigie

Osanobua.myth: Contest for divine status and wealth
Osanobua.note: Some Edo narratives have Olókun compete for status, wealth, or a spouse.
Osanobua.source: Edo oral accounts collected by Izevbigie

Oshun Ipondá.myth: Oshun disguises herself to attract Erinle
Oshun Ipondá.note: She uses honey and forest matter to attract Erinle, conceiving Logun Edé before he leaves.
Erinle and Oshun Ipondá conceive Logun Edé in a Brazilian narrative.

Otin.note: Some Yoruba and Brazilian accounts associate Otin with Erinle as his wife.
Other accounts present Otin as Erinle's companion or closely related hunter-river power.
Some houses fuse Otin with Oshosi, though other regions preserve a separate identity.

Our Lady of Mercy.note: Lucumí tradition pairs Obatalá with the white-robed Virgin of Mercy.

Our Lady of Mount Carmel.note: Verger records a Cuban Catholic correspondence between Naná Burukú and Our Lady of Mount Carmel.

Our Lady of Regla.note: Cuban devotion historically identifies or ritually pairs Yemayá with the Black Madonna.

Oxaguiã.note: Oxaguiã manifests after the Bayanni-crown procession and participates in the ritual succession.
Brazilian theology incorporates the Ejigbo deity as the youthful path of Oxalá.

Oxalufã.note: Oxalufã manifests with Oxaguiã after the Bayanni-crown procession.

Oṣagiyan.note: Some Brazilian houses report shared ritual foundations between Logun Edé and Oṣagiyan.

Polo.note: Polo serves as Oko's executioner, killing people Oko judges guilty of witchcraft.

Pombagiras.note: Èṣù-related terminology and imagery influenced this distinct Brazilian class of female spirits.

Ram.note: Personified Ram betrays or exposes Ọya, causing hostility and a dietary taboo.

Saint Anne.note: Brazilian syncretism identifies Nanã with the venerable grandmother Saint Anne.

Saint Anthony of Padua.note: Some Cuban houses identify Elegguá with Saint Anthony of Padua.
Bahian practice corresponds Ogum with Saint Anthony, partly through the saint's military career.

Saint Barbara.note: Cuban tradition pairs Changó with Saint Barbara through lightning, royal, and red-and-white imagery.

Saint Catherine of Alexandria.note: Brazilian syncretistic lists commonly pair Oba with Catherine of Alexandria.

Saint Catherine of Siena.note: Some English summaries pair Oba with Catherine of Siena.

Saint Francis of Assisi.note: Some Brazilian houses correspond Iroko with Saint Francis of Assisi.

Saint George.note: Brazilian practice corresponds Ogum with Saint George through weapons, metal, courage, and protection.

Saint Jerome.note: Some Afro-Brazilian regions or nations locally equate Xangô with Saint Jerome.

Saint John the Baptist.note: Some Afro-Brazilian traditions locally equate Xangô with Saint John the Baptist.

Saint Julian.note: Venezuelan transmission of Cuban Santería identifies Inle with Saint Julian.

Saint Lawrence.note: Some Brazilian houses correspond Iroko with Saint Lawrence.

Saint Martin de Porres.note: Some Cuban traditions associate Elegguá with Saint Martin through complexion and service imagery.

Saint Michael.note: Some Afro-Brazilian traditions locally equate Xangô with Saint Michael.

Saint Peter.note: Cuban practice corresponds Ogun with Saint Peter through keys, iron, imprisonment, and iconography.

Saint Raphael the Archangel.note: Cuban tradition identifies Inle with Raphael through healing, blindness, and fish symbolism.

Saint Roch.note: Some Cuban traditions identify Inle with Saint Roch through healing and disease.

Saint Sebastian.note: Some Brazilian traditions, including Recife, identify him with Saint Sebastian through the saint's wounded body.

Saint Teresa.note: Verger records Saint Teresa as a Cuban Catholic correspondence for Naná Burukú.

San Lázaro.note: Cuban devotion historically identifies Babalú-Ayé with overlapping figures called Lazarus.

San Ramón Nonato.note: Other Cuban sources identify Dadá or Obañeñe with the childbirth-associated saint.

Santa Bárbara.note: Brazilian traditions identify or ritually pair Ọya with the lightning-bearing saint.

Santa Clara.note: Eastern Cuban traditions sometimes identify Ọya with Santa Clara.

Santa Clara de Asís.note: Some Cuban and Brazilian tables identify Yewá with Santa Clara.

Santa Teresa de Jesús.note: Cuban Lucumí traditions identify Ọya with this cemetery-associated saint.

Santo Niño de Atocha.note: Cuban devotees associate Elegguá’s child form and traveler protection with Santo Niño.

Somú Gagá.note: Somú Gagá accompanies Olokun and represents life, masking, or the living aspect of the abyss.

St Bartholomew.note: Bahian Candomblé associates Oxumaré with St Bartholomew and his August feast.

São Roque.note: Brazilian traditions identify him with the plague-protecting saint marked by bodily sores.

Tempo.note: Brazilian houses align Iroko with Tempo through shared tree, duration, and outdoor symbolism.

Tòròsì.note: Oyo tradition names the Nupe or Tapa princess Tòròsì as Ṣàngó’s mother.
Tòròsì.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

Umbanda Exus.note: Èṣù’s name and functions helped name Brazilian spirit classes ordinarily understood as human dead.

Virgen de la Candelaria.note: Havana and some Lucumí lists identify Ọya with Candelaria.

Virgen de los Dolores.note: Some Cuban houses identify Yewá with this Marian figure.

Virgen del Carmen.note: Eastern Cuban traditions sometimes identify Ọya with Virgen del Carmen.

Yahweh.note: Christian theology and Yoruba Bible translation identify Olodumare or Ọlọ́run with Yahweh.

Yemanjá.note: Yemanjá forbids Oxóssi to enter the forest where Ossaim awaits him.

Yembó.note: One Cuban genealogy names Inle as the son of Yembó and Obatalá.
Some Cuban lineages identify Yembó as Oba’s mother.

Yemowo.note: A mythic-historical interpretation associates Nanã with Yemowo in the old water-mud order.

Yemòó.note: Ifẹ shrine and festival traditions treat Yemòó as Obatala’s spouse or female counterpart.

Yemú.note: Ozun guards the household Yemú shares with Obatalá.
Some Cuban manuals and internet traditions call Ozun a son of Yemú.

Zambi.note: Some Umbanda schools place Olorum alongside the Bantu supreme being Zambi.

a Valkyrie.note: Modern comparativists equate Ọya with a generic Valkyrie.

guardian angel.note: Cuban Catholic terminology translates Orí or Eledá as a guardian angel.

sister of Oyá.note: A delicate sister of Oyá reportedly lives at Iroko’s foot and receives sacrifice.

sixteen male ìrúnmọlẹ̀.myth: The excluded woman and failed creation
sixteen male ìrúnmọlẹ̀.note: They exclude Ọ̀ṣun, and their creative projects fail until she participates.

the Hermetic All.note: Modern occult writers equate Olodumare with the Hermetic All.

the collective òrìṣà.note: Orí defeats or outranks the assembled òrìṣà after a test or journey.

the individual’s tutelary òrìṣà.note: The tutelary òrìṣà owns the ritual head but cannot bless without Orí’s consent.

the irúnmọlẹ̀.note: Olodumare assembles or sends the divinities and assigns their powers and domains.

the orixás.note: Modern Brazilian theology makes Iroko the route by which the orixás descended to Ayé.

the other orishas.note: The other orishas seize scattered leaves but still depend on Ossaim's activating knowledge.
In another version, Ossaim voluntarily gives each orisha one leaf.

the three blackbirds.myth: Oko of Irawo and the crop-devouring birds
the three blackbirds.note: Oko uses powerful medicine to expel three blackbirds repeatedly destroying Irawo's harvest.

the òrìṣà.note: Later theology calls Yemoja their literal or honorific universal mother.

Àjà.note: Regional accounts associate Àjà with Ossaim's acquisition of wilderness medicine.

Àjàlá.note: Àjàlá molds or stores the Orí selected by the prenatal person.

Àjẹ́.note: Some Ifá verses describe witches as deploying Ajogun, although the two adversarial classes remain distinct.
Ọ̀rúnmìlà negotiates with the powerful mothers and prescribes offerings to secure cooperation.
He is called their husband, signifying ritual authority or alliance rather than ordinary marriage.

Àrònì.note: Regional traditions make Àrònì a teacher or source of Ossaim's medicinal knowledge.
Àrònì and Ọ̀sányìn are associated through shared forest and medicinal knowledge.

Àrùn.note: Àrùn, Disease, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Àwọn Ìyá.note: Ossaim's iron staff acknowledges, controls, or counters the Mothers' dangerous bird power.

Èpè.note: Èpè, Curse, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Èṣe.note: Èṣe, Affliction, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Èṣù.note: After Iroko sacrifices, Èṣù has hostile trees felled while ordering farmers to spare Iroko.
Èṣù.source: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus

Èṣù.note: Èṣù substitutes a goat’s head and prevents Iroko from collecting the promised child.
Èṣù receives or conveys offerings and mediates between humans, divinities, and the Mothers.

Èṣù.myth: Palm wine placed on Obatala’s road
Èṣù.note: Some variants say Èṣù provides or sells the palm wine causing Obatala’s failure.
Èṣù receives precedence and carries sacrifices in various Obatala narratives.
Èṣù repeatedly soils and burdens Oxalufã during his difficult journey.

Èṣù.myth: Èṣù conveys sacrifices and enforces compliance
Èṣù.note: Èṣù mediates the Odù’s prescriptions, carries offerings, tests compliance, and affects results.
Èṣù facilitates Ọbàtálá’s intoxication or confusion, indirectly enabling Oduduwa’s succession.
Èṣù carries or enforces the sacrifice enabling Orí’s success.
Èṣù carries prescribed sacrifices and enforces the outcomes revealed by Ọ̀rúnmìlà.
Èṣù tests or inconveniences Ọ̀rúnmìlà in recurring divinatory narratives.
Èṣù collapses a building on Ọ̀sányìn for neglected sacrifice or precedence.
Èṣù appears as messenger or agent in stories concerning Ọya.
Èṣù appears as ritual messenger in sacrifice contexts involving Yemoja.

Ìkú.note: Èṣù evades or redirects Death through quick speech, bargaining, or transformation.

Ìsédalẹ̀.note: Johnson names Ìsédalẹ̀ as a child of Oduduwa and Ọlọ́kun.

Ìyámi.myth: Powerful mothers are appeased or opposed
Ìyámi.note: Depending on the verse, the Odù prescribe appeasing, respecting, or opposing the powerful mothers.
Oshosi defeats the monstrous bird sent or inhabited by the female powers.

Ìyámi Oshoronga.note: One Cuban genealogy includes Ìyámi Oshoronga among Yewá's siblings.

Ìyámi Oshoronga.myth: Flight from Yewá's cemetery to Olókun's sea
Ìyámi Oshoronga.note: She flies between Yewá's cemetery and Olókun's sea.

Òfò.note: Òfò, Loss, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Òsá Méjì.note: Òsá Méjì carries the Mother from heaven toward earth inside his body.
The Mother refuses to leave his abdomen until goat viscera draw her out.

àbíkú.note: Large iroko trees are associated with companies of recurrently dying and returning àbíkú children.

Ẹ̀gbà.note: Ẹ̀gbà, Paralysis, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Ẹ̀là.myth: Ẹ̀là voices the efficacy of Ifá
Ẹ̀là.note: Ẹ̀là is invoked as Ifá’s saving voice or manifestation, though its ontology varies.

Ẹ̀wọ̀n.note: Ẹ̀wọ̀n, Imprisonment, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Ọ̀kọ́.note: Some traditions add Ọ̀kọ́ among Ọya's husbands or lovers.

Ọ̀ràn.note: Ọ̀ràn, Great Trouble, appears as a principal co-member in the canonical enumeration and concerted assaults.

Ọ̀rànmíyàn.note: Dada/Ajaka is the eldest son of Ọ̀yọ́’s dynastic founder Ọ̀rànmíyàn.
Ọ̀rànmíyàn.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

Ọ̀rànmíyàn.note: Johnson names Ọ̀rànmíyàn as a child of Oduduwa and Ọlọ́kun.
Other dynastic traditions make Ọ̀rànmíyàn Oduduwa’s grandson or more distant descendant.
Ọ̀rànmíyàn carries Oduduwa’s dynastic legitimacy to Ọ̀yọ́ and Benin.
Oyo royal genealogy names Ọ̀rànmíyàn as Ṣàngó’s father.
Ọ̀rànmíyàn.source: Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

Ọ̀rúngan.note: Ellis places Ṣàngó among offspring produced by Ọ̀rúngan’s union with Yemọja.

Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì.note: Ọ̀rúnmìlà joins Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì and Ògún in rescue, hunting, and problem-solving stories.
Some traditions add Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì among Ọya's husbands or lovers.
The hunter deity Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì emerges from Yemoja.
